title: The unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21–35)
hookLine: forgiven a fortune, he throttles a man who owes him pocket change
tomorrow: the Pharisee and the tax collector

cards: Peter thinks he's being generous. How many times do I have to forgive my brother? Seven times?
Jesus says: not seven. "Until seventy times seven." Then he tells a story.
A king is settling his accounts, and a servant is brought in who owes ten thousand talents. That's the talent from two days ago; ten thousand is a debt no servant could ever pay.
The king orders him sold, with his wife and children. The servant falls on his knees and begs for time. The king, moved with compassion, doesn't give him time.

teach.h: HE TOOK HIM BY THE THROAT.
teach.b: In the old King James Bible, he "took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest." A hundred silver coins was real money; in the vineyard story, one coin was a day's wage.
Next to what he'd just been let off, it's pocket change.

And the other man falls down and begs with almost the same words: have patience with me, and I will pay thee all. That echo is the point. He hears his own prayer coming back at him, and doesn't recognize it.
He has the man thrown in prison. The other servants, upset, go to the king.

teach.h: AS I HAD PITY ON THEE.
teach.b: The king calls him back and asks: "Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?" The ending is hard.
The king hands him over to be punished until he pays, and Jesus says the Father will do the same to anyone who doesn't forgive from the heart.

Christians don't soften that, but they often hear the warning as the flip side of the gift: mercy received is meant to keep moving. It's the shape of the Lord's Prayer: forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.
The Greek of Jesus's answer to Peter can be read as seventy times seven or seventy-seven, and translators still differ.

teach.h: MERCY IS MEANT TO KEEP MOVING.
teach.b: Either way it means: stop counting. Some Christian teachers add that forgiving a debt doesn't mean pretending it didn't happen, or staying where you'll be hurt. It means letting go of the throat.

how: Christians ask God's forgiveness and pledge to forgive others every time they pray the Lord's Prayer ("forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors"), and churches often read this parable when teaching about forgiveness and reconciliation.

o: a fortune in silver, a huge sum
a written record of what is owed
a yearly tax a king collects

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: moved with compassion, canceled it all

s: Jesus tells Peter to forgive seven times
Peter suggests seven. Jesus says seventy times seven, or seventy-seven: stop counting.
both debtors beg with nearly the same words
have patience with me, and I will pay thee all. the echo is the whole point.
the king gives the first servant more time to pay
he asked for time. the king canceled the whole debt.

games.q: you've just been let off a debt you could never repay. in the street, a man who owes you a hundred silver coins begs for time. what do you do?
o: let it go, the way the king did.
grab him by the throat and have him jailed until he pays.
games.why: he "took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest," and had him thrown in prison. the other servants were so upset they told the king.

practice: Remember a time someone could have held something over you and didn't: a friend who never mentioned the money, a teacher who gave you another chance.
Stay with how it felt to walk out free; if you pray, give thanks for them, and if you don't, rest in the gratitude. Then, gently, notice who owes you something small.

wordCard.voice: Talent. A fortune in silver, the coin so large that ten thousand of them was a debt no servant could ever hope to repay.

orig.note: Greek: to let go, release. the same verb is used for forgiving a debt and forgiving a sin.

carryVoice: Your line: pass the mercy on. Mercy that stops with you isn't finished. Rest well tonight.
